senses.gloss:
Education
------------------------------------------
Introduction
The उपनिषद्स् aver that whatever good is done with full knowledge and awareness becomes forceful and fruitful in life. भर्तृहरि, a well-known Sanskrit poet, compares a man without any एदुचतिओन् to a brute. Albert Einstein (A. D.1879-1955) seems to concur with him when he likens a man with a specialized knowledge, but lacking in values, to a well-trained dog!
Vivekānanda, the great patriot-prophet of Modern India, who could feel the pulse of the Indian nation, states that:
Education is the panacea for all our ills.
It is the manifestation of the perfection already in man.
It is the training by which the current and expression of will are brought under control and become fruitful in life.
It is life-building, man-making, character-making assimilation of ideas.
It is rather astonishing that many Western savants 1 have practically echoed Vivekānanda’s ideas though in different words.
These can be briefly summarized as follows:
Education should teach our children self-control, the art of holding one’s passions and prejudices.
It should instil true and worthy motives, a profound religious feeling and inspire the formation of a great character.
It should help us to understand the laws of God in nature and to shape our lives to be in consonance with those laws.
It should pay much greater attention to the development of the powers of the मिन्द् than mere learning of facts.
The ancient and medieval systems of एदुचतिओन् recognized all these aspects while formulating the policies guiding them. Accordingly all fields of विद्या or knowledge were divided into two broad streams: the parāvidyā (the higher know-ledge, the spiritual wisdom) and the aparāvidyā (the lower knowledge, the secular sciences). The latter is needed to live a comfortable life here. The former helps one to be fully prepared for the hereafter. Hence a balanced combination of both, is advocated so that both civilization and culture are imparted.
It is very interesting to note that even an ancient Upaniṣad—the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—assigned to the period 4000 B. C. to 2500 B. C., mentions as many as fifteen branches of knowledge apart from the four वेदस्! Some of them are: व्याकरण (grammar), Pitrya (science of obsequial rites), Gaṇita (mathematics), दैव (knowledge of the portents), तर्क (logic), एकायन (ethics), भूतविद्या (science of the spirits), धनुर्वेद (martial arts and sciences), ज्यौतिष (astronomy) and Devajanavidyā (the art of preparing perfumes, मुसिच्, dancing and sculpture).
Constituents of an Educational System
The three constituents of an educational system are: the teacher, the student and the content as also the methods of एदुचतिओन्.
A spiritual teacher—generally called ‘guru’ or ‘ācārya’ गुरु and the आचार्य do not.">2—was expected to be a ‘śrotriya’ (learned in the वेदस् and allied scriptures) and a ‘brahmaniṣṭha’ (well-established in ब्रह्मन् or God). As applied to other fields of knowledge it could mean that he should be an expert both in theory and in practice. An impeccable character, earnestness to teach and a genuine love towards the student were the additional qualities expected in him.
Eagerness to learn, humility, obedience to the teacher, self-control, absence of laziness in the pursuit of knowledge and willingness to do personal service to the teacher—these were the essential traits a student must possess, to qualify for admission.
Gurukulas
The teachers kept their students in their own houses. When the number of students became large, these houses would grow into institutions called ‘gurukulas,’ established by the society, the kings and the rich endowing them with sufficient property and funds so that they could provide quality एदुचतिओन्, free of cost, to all the students.
As a result, these gurukulas or educational academies grew to enormous dimensions—both in quality and quantity—thus fulfilling the significance of their very names: गुरु = enormous, कुल = institution. It was not uncommon to find as many as ten thousand students in some of these bigger institutions. Not only out of necessity, but also as a good practice, the senior and better qualified students were made to teach the novices and also supervise over their life and discipline. Though punishments for transgressions existed they were not very severe. Incorrigible students were expelled to save the discipline and reputation of the institution.
For imparting parāvidyā or spiritual wisdom, an earnest desire to learn and a willingness to undergo तपस् or austerity were the only requirements. Neither वर्ण nor आश्रम nor age seems to have mattered.
However, for the study of the वेदस् and allied sciences like the वेदाङ्गस्, वेदस्.' They are six: शिक्षा (phonetics); छन्दस् (prosody); व्याकरण (grammar); निरुक्त (etymology); कल्प (liturgics); ज्यौतिष (astronomy).">3 some restrictions had been imposed. It was open only to the dvijas (the ‘twice-born,’ the members of the first three castes) and that too after the boys had undergone the उपनयन यज्ञोपवीत, and the receiving of the holy Gāyatrīmantra are the primary aspects of this sacrament.">4 ceremony.
Now, some additional, but miscellaneous, information can be given to get a more complete picture of the system over the centuries:
Scholarly disputations and philosophical discussions used to take place even in the Vedic period, in meetings generally known as ‘samiti’ or ‘samāja’ or ‘pariṣad’.
Vārāṇasī or काशी and तक्षशिला were well-known as great centres of learning even from the 8th century B. C. Some cities like Pāṭalīputra, Vidiśā and काञ्चीपुरम् were called ‘ghaṭikāsthānas,’ centres capable of measuring the scholarship of the savants. In such centres there was provision to get training in 14 to 18 branches of learning. 5 Students were free to acquire a deep knowledge of their religion without any hindrance from the followers of other religions.
The universities of तक्षशिला (400 B. C.), Vikramaśilā (A. D. 800) and नालन्दा (A. D. 600) had attained phenomenal growth and fame. These universities had several mahāpāṭhaśālās (colleges) and each of these again comprised several lecture halls. There were three huge buildings housing big libraries of invaluable manuscripts.
Admission tests were very strict and only 20% of the aspirants could succeed in getting admission.
In the नालन्दा University alone there were 8500 students, taught by 1500 teachers with at least 100 lectures delivered per day. Professors like नागार्जुन, Vasubandhu and Diṅnāga were internationally reputed scholars attracting a large number of students from many foreign countries like China, Japan, Korea, Turkestan, Burma, गान्धार (Afghanisthan), Sumātra and Persia. Though एदुचतिओन् was mostly residential and free, students who could afford to pay, did so.
Among the residential students Buddhist nuns were also there. However, according to Hiuen Tsang (A. D. 600-664) and I-Tsing (A. D. 635-713), not even a single instance of misconduct had been noticed or discovered, thanks to the high degree of moral discipline kept up by the teachers and the administrators.
Apart from these Buddhist universities, we learn from कौटिल्य (300 B. C.) and others that there were industrial and vocational training institutions too, impar-ting specialized training in those branches.
From all these accounts we find that the educational system of the ancient and medieval India was not only highly developed but also capable of delivering to us a lesson or two even now.
Script, Language and Literature
A passing reference may now be made to some allied topics like the evolution of the script, language and literature. The art of writing was known even during the Vedic age though memorization was preferred and encouraged. The two scripts—Brāhmī and Kharoṣṭhī—are known to have existed even in 600 B. C. Both the देवनागरी and some of the South Indian scripts are its evolutes. Tālapatra (palm-leaf), Bhūrjapatra (birch-bark), wooden plates, cloth (of cotton or silk), leather, stone and bricks were used for writing.
Evidence is not lacking to conclude that Sanskrit works existed even as early as 600 to 100 B. C. Apart from the वेदस्, the epics—the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahā-bhārata—stand out as monuments of exquisitely beautiful literature of a very high standard. The ease and facility with which the सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे has been used even in the composition of technical subjects bearing on liturgy, medical and health sciences, एथिच्स् or linguistics, is astounding.
The प्राकृत् language—a popular deri-vative of Sanskrit—also had been fairly well-developed even by 500 B. C.
The following table gives the approximate periods of the evolution of the earliest literary works in other Indian languages:
Assamese: A. D. 1300
Bengali: A. D. 1100
Gujarati: A. D. 1000
Hindi: A. D. 1000
Kannada: A. D. 100
Kashmiri: A. D. 1200
Malayalam: A. D. 900
Marathi: A. D. 1000
Oriya: A. D. 700
Punjabi: A. D. 1000
Sindhi: A. D. 1000
Tamil: 600 B. C.
Telugu: 200 B. C.
Urdu: A. D. 1300

A few important literary works in these languages composed during the early and the medieval periods may now be cited:
Works of Hemasarasvatī, हरिहर विप्र and शङ्कर Deva in Assamese; the मङ्गल and the विजय literature in Bengali; works of Narasī Mehtā and रामानन्द in Gujarati; compositions of Tulasīdas, Mīrā, विद्यापति and कबीर् in Hindi; grammar and mythological literature of Keśirāja, Pampa, Ranna and हरिहर as also the religious literature of the Śivaśaraṇas and Haridāsas of Kannada; works of Jñāneśvar, Eknāth, तुकाराम् and others in Marathi; Pañcasakhās’ works in Oriya; the Guru-Granth Sāhīb in Punjabi; the Kuraḷ of तिरुवऌऌउवर्, the Tevārams and the Divyaprabandhams of Tamil saints in Tamil; the poetical works of Śrīnātha, Potana, Vemana and अण्णमाचार्य in Telugu.
From all these, we can conclude that the Indian languages and literature had attained considerable growth and refinement even by the middle ages.
